extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent prosecution practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive guidance for determining, applying, and overcoming rejections under 35 U.S.C. 102 (printed publication, patent, public use, on sale, etc.), including rules for effective filing dates, use of abstracts, and treatment of international applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of abstracts versus underlying documents
rubrics_metrics.description: When an abstract is used to support a rejection, the evidence relied upon is the facts contained in the abstract, not additional facts in the underlying full text document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citation of and reliance upon an abstract without citation of and reliance upon the underlying scientific document is generally inappropriate where both the abstract and the underlying document are prior art. To determine whether both qualify as prior art, obtain and analyze a copy of the underlying document. If the document is not in English and the examiner seeks to rely on it, a translation must be obtained so the record is clear as to the precise facts relied upon. The record must state whether the examiner is relying on the abstract or the full text document.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for underlying document when both abstract and full text are prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: When both the abstract and the underlying document qualify as prior art, the underlying document should normally be used to support a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In limited circumstances an examiner may make a non-final Office action rejection based in whole or in part on the abstract only without relying on the full text document, but the full text and translation (if not English) should be supplied in the next Office action. Whether the next Office action may be made final is governed by MPEP § 706.07(a). Rationale: full text can reveal anticipation or teachings away not apparent in the abstract; abstracts may have different effective publication dates than the full text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between 35 U.S.C. 102 (anticipation) and 35 U.S.C. 103 (obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: For anticipation under 35 U.S.C. 102 the reference must teach every aspect of the claimed invention either explicitly or implicitly; any feature not directly taught must be inherently present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 the reference teachings must be modified to meet the claims and the modification must be one that would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made. See MPEP §§ 2131–2146 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the effective filing date of the application
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective filing date is determined by the application's relationship to earlier filings and whether statutory requirements for benefit/priority are satisfied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules: (A) If continuation/divisional and 35 U.S.C. 120/365(c) satisfied, effective date is the earlier filing date. (B) If continuation-in-part (CIP), claims not supported by parent get the new application's filing date; claims supported under 35 U.S.C. 112 by the parent have the parent's date. (C) If claiming foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d)/365(a)/(b), effective filing date is the U.S. filing date unless (A) or (B) applies; the foreign priority filing date is not the effective filing date though it may be used as a reference to overcome rejections. (D) If claiming 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to a provisional, the provisional filing date is effective for claims fully supported by the provisional under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph. See MPEP cross-references for PCT/371 issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine which 35 U.S.C. 102 subsection to apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a printed publication or patent is found, determine whether to make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(a), (b) or (e) by comparing the reference date with the application's effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First determine the issue or publication date of the reference (e.g., magazines are effective when they reach the addressee), then compare with the application's effective filing date per MPEP § 706.02. See MPEP §§ 707.05(f), 2124, 2126, 2128–2128.02 for reference date case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining the issue or publication date of a reference
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must determine the issue or publication date so a proper comparison with the application's effective filing date can be made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a magazine is effective as of the date it reached the addressee, not the mailing date. For foreign patents see MPEP § 901.05. Use relevant MPEP sections and case law to establish reference dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying 35 U.S.C. 102(b) (statutory bar)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider 35 U.S.C. 102(b) first because it results in a statutory bar if the publication or issue date of the reference is more than one year prior to the application's effective filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the last day of the 1-year period falls on Saturday, Sunday, or a Federal holiday, the publication is not a statutory bar if the application was filed the next succeeding business day (Ex parte Olah). Changes to 37 CFR 1.6(a)(2) and 1.10 do not affect applicant’s concurrent right to defer filing to the next business day in such situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applying 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference is too recent for 102(b), consider 35 U.S.C. 102(e); to apply 102(e) the inventive entity of the application must be different than that of the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there are joint inventors, only one inventor need be different for inventive entities to be different and for a 102(e) rejection to be applicable even if some inventors are in common. Revised 102(e) (AIPA and later amendments) applies retroactively as described in the MPEP; international application exceptions (filed prior to Nov 29, 2000) are handled specially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revised 35 U.S.C. 102(e) treatment of international applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the revised statute, an international filing date on or after November 29, 2000 is a U.S. filing date for prior art purposes under 35 U.S.C. 102(e) only if three conditions are met.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The three conditions: (a) international filing date on or after Nov 29, 2000; (b) the international application designated the United States; and (c) it was published under PCT Article 21(2) in English by WIPO. If all are met, the international filing date can be used as the prior art date; if not, treat the reference under earlier rules or as 102(a)/(b) as appropriate. Publications or patents from international applications filed before Nov 29, 2000 are subject to pre-AIPA rules and may not have a 102(e) date at all (but may be prior art under 102(a) or (b) by publication date).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider 35 U.S.C. 102(a) even if reference qualifies under 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a reference qualifies under 102(e), the examiner should still consider 35 U.S.C. 102(a) for two reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First, for U.S. patents or application publications of, or claiming benefit of, an international application, the PCT Article 21(2) publication may be the earliest prior art date under 102(a). Second, references only prior art under 102(e)/(f)/(g) applied in a rejection under 103 may be subject to 103(c) if the reference and the application were commonly owned or subject to an obligation of common assignment at the time the invention was made; 102(a) may avoid such disqualification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(b) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A 102(b) rejection can be overcome by procedural or claim-focused actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible responses include: (A) Persuasively arguing that the claims are patentably distinguishable from the prior art; (B) Amending the claims to patentably distinguish over the prior art; (C) Perfecting priority under 35 U.S.C. 120 (within time set in 37 CFR 1.78(a)) by amending the specification or filing an application data sheet and establishing the earlier application's compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph; or (D) Perfecting priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) to a provisional (with caveats about chains of intermediate applications and timing). See MPEP §201.11 for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(e) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: A 102(e) rejection may be overcome by arguments, amendments, affidavits/declarations, or priority claims, subject to limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include: (A) Persuasive argument of patentable distinction; (B) Amend claims; (C) File affidavit/declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 showing the reference invention is not by 'another'; (D) File 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit/declaration showing prior invention if the reference is not a U.S. patent or U.S. application publication claiming the same patentable invention (1.131 is not acceptable if reference U.S. patent or U.S. publication and application claim same invention or obvious variants; then double patenting or interference may be appropriate); (E) Perfect foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d) within 37 CFR 1.55(a)(1) time or petition; (F) Perfect priority under 119(e) or 120 within 37 CFR 1.78(a) time or petition, ensuring enablement and written description under 35 U.S.C. 112, first paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to overcome a 35 U.S.C. 102(a) rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: 102(a) rejections can be overcome by arguments, amendments, affidavits/declarations, or priority claims, subject to limitations analogous to 102(e) guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include: (A) Persuasive argument of patentable distinction; (B) Amend claims; (C) File 37 CFR 1.131 affidavit/declaration showing prior invention if the reference is not a U.S. patent or U.S. application publication claiming the same patentable invention (1.131 is not appropriate when claims of the reference and the application are directed to the same invention or obvious variants); (D) File 37 CFR 1.132 affidavit/declaration showing the reference invention is not by 'another'; (E) Perfect foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(a)-(d); (F) Perfect priority under 119(e) or 120 as explained for 102(e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use or on sale evidence (35 U.S.C. 102(a) or (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When applicant admission, evidence of sale, knowledge by others, or examiner's personal knowledge indicates public use or sale, determine whether 102(a) or 102(b) applies and gather necessary information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'In this country' means the United States only (not other WTO or NAFTA countries). If activity is by another entity, both 102(a) and 102(b) may be applicable. If evidence points to knowledge within one year of effective filing date, 102(a) applies; if activity occurred more than one year prior, 102(b) applies. Do not make 102(a) rejection if evidence shows applicant made the invention and disclosed it to others within the year prior to filing. Examiner may require applicant to answer specific questions and supplement evidence per 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.104(a)(2); information sought should be restricted to what is reasonably necessary. Examiner may use 37 CFR 1.105 requirement for information where reasonably necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for information re: public use or on sale (Form paragraph 7.104)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an issue of public use or on-sale activity is raised, the examiner may issue a requirement for information to properly consider patentability under 35 U.S.C. 102(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form paragraph 7.104 reminds applicant failure to fully reply can result in abandonment. Examiner notes: (1) Information sought should be restricted to what is reasonably necessary for a patentability decision (see MPEP §2133.03). (2) A one- or two-month reply period should be set unless part of an Office action having a shortened statutory period (SSP). (3) If sufficient evidence exists to establish a prima facie case of public use or on sale, use form paragraph 7.16 to make a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(b). Failure to timely reply to the requirement may result in abandonment (35 U.S.C. 133).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(c) – abandonment of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 35 U.S.C. 102(c), abandonment of the 'invention' (distinct from abandonment of an application) results in loss of right to a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2134 for case law and criteria clarifying abandonment under 102(c).

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(d) – four conditions for statutory bar and searching guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: 102(d) establishes four conditions which, if all present, create a statutory bar to grant of a U.S. patent based on a foreign patent/application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four conditions: (A) foreign application filed more than 12 months before the U.S. effective filing date; (B) foreign and U.S. applications filed by same applicant/legal representatives/assigns; (C) foreign application actually issued as a patent or inventor's certificate before U.S. filing (need not be published); (D) the same invention is involved. Examiner should only search for a granted foreign patent for 102(d) prior art if there is a reasonable possibility that a foreign patent covering the same subject matter has been granted to the same inventive entity before the U.S. effective filing date (because pendency varies by country). The search can be done via electronic databases by examiner or STIC staff. The document relied upon must be a patent or inventor's certificate, not merely a published/laid-open application. See MPEP §2135.01 and §901.06(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination guidelines for applying references under 35 U.S.C. 102(e)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the appropriate 102(e) date for each potential reference by following stepwise guidelines: verify reference type, check international application relationship, and apply date rules depending on international filing characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: I. (A) Potential reference must be U.S. patent, U.S. application publication (35 U.S.C. 122(b)), or WIPO publication of international application under PCT Article 21(2). (B) Determine if reference resulted from or claimed benefit of an international application; if yes, proceed to (C). (C) If resulted from/claimed benefit of an international application: (1) If international filing date on/after Nov 29, 2000 AND designated the U.S. AND published under PCT Art 21(2) in English, then international filing date is a U.S. filing date for 102(e) purposes (and may be bridged to earlier applications if appropriate and supported under 35 U.S.C. 112); (2) If filed on/after Nov 29, 2000 but did not designate the U.S. or was not published in English under PCT Art 21(2), do not treat international filing date as U.S. filing date—apply as 102(a)/(b) by publication date or 102(e) as of any later U.S. filing date that properly claimed benefit; (3) If international filing date prior to Nov 29, 2000, apply pre-AIPA provisions (e.g., for U.S. patents, 102(e) date is earlier of completion of 371(c)(1),(2),(4) or filing date of later-filed U.S. application that claimed benefit; U.S. application publications/WIPO publications directly resulting from international apps filed before Nov 29, 2000 are never applied under 102(e) but may be 102(a)/(b) by publication date; etc.); (4) Be aware that a WIPO publication may have an earlier 102(a)/(b) date even if a related U.S. patent/application does not have an earlier 102(e) date. (D) Foreign applications' filing dates claimed via 35 U.S.C. 119/365 may not be used as 102(e) dates; international filing dates claimed as foreign priority under 365(a)/(b) are likewise not usable as 102(e) dates. II. Examples (nine illustrative examples) are provided to illustrate common factual situations for determining 102(e) dates; use examples only as illustrations, not definitive rules for all fact patterns.
